Quagmire

/KWAG-myre/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Quagmire means a difficult, tangled situation that is hard to escape — like soft, boggy ground that holds your boots fast.

The border war that the generals promised would take six weeks became a decade-long quagmire that drained the empire's treasury and patience.

Worked Example

After a week of rain, the shortcut across the pasture turned into a quagmire that gripped the hikers' boots at every step.

The ground literally holds the hikers fast and makes each step harder than the last — the physical stuckness that gives quagmire its figurative meaning.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

predicament: a difficult, unpleasant situation

impasse: a deadlock with no way forward

bind: a tight spot that is hard to get out of

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

breeze: something effortlessly easy to get through

cinch: a task that is simple and certain

Where it sits · how long the work stays trapped — snag → quagmire → black hole

snag vs. quagmire: A snag costs you an hour or a day; a quagmire holds the whole project fast for months.

black hole vs. quagmire: Calling a project a black hole is even bleaker than calling it a quagmire — a quagmire might still release you eventually, but a black hole devours money and effort with no end in sight.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — quag

Root — quag: boggy, shaking ground (an old English word, likely related to quake)

Root — mire

Root — mire: deep, sticky mud (from Old Norse myrr)

Put it together

Put it together: Quag (shaking, boggy ground, likely a relative of quake) plus mire (deep mud) builds the literal picture: ground that trembles and swallows — exactly what a figurative quagmire does to wars, lawsuits, and projects.

Use the root in a new word: mire

Use the root in a new word: mire: One wrong step off the boardwalk left her ankle-deep in the mire.

Word Choice

Neutral; common in journalism and history

Quagmire is the go-to word for a costly effort that was easy to start and is nearly impossible to leave — writers use it constantly for stalled wars, lawsuits, and construction projects. Unlike a morass (which buries you in confusion) or a maelstrom (which batters you with churning violence), the heart of quagmire is stuckness: every motion sinks you deeper.
